newsitem.title: USA: Book by Clinton guru raises questions about polls.
newsitem.headline: Book by Clinton guru raises questions about polls.

text.p: By Alan Elsner, Political Correspondent
Former Clinton White House guru Dick Morris says opinion polls govern almost every aspect of President Bill Clinton's behaviour, from the colour of his ties to where he goes on holiday.
Is this an expansion or an abuse of democracy, and what does it say about political leadership in the United States?

Morris was forced to resign from an influential position in Clinton's re-election campaign last August when it was disclosed he had had a year-long affair with a prostitute and even showed her confidential campaign documents .

He spells out his role as Clinton's intimate adviser in a new book, "Behind the Oval Office," for which he was paid $2.5 million. Though dismissed by some critics as self-serving and unreliable, the book does raise serious questions.
"From the beginning of our relationship in 1977, polls have been my common frame of reference with Bill Clinton," Morris writes.
He paints a portrait of a president and a White House obsessed with polling, ordering snapshots of public opinion virtually every single day.

Clinton, says Morris, knows every detail of every poll. "A poll helps him sense who doesn't like him and why they don't ... For Bill Clinton, positive poll results are vindication, ratification and approval, whereas negative poll results are a learning process in which the pain of the rebuff to his self-image forces deep introspection."

Clinton consults polls as if they were "giant windsocks that tell him which way the wind is blowing. And then he asks the pollster to help him determine which current he should try to harnass to move him closer to his destination," he says.

White House spokesman Mike McCurry said Clinton had read the book with interest. "Parts of it are interesting, parts of it are wrong, parts are factually off the mark, some of it provides insights," McCurry said, without getting specific.

Morris says even he himself sometimes took polling too far as when he used data to tell Clinton what he should do during his August vacation. "I urged that he take a mountain vacation, that he hike and camp out in a tent."
Clinton groused about the advice but ended up accepting it and then complained that his favourability rating had dropped by a point while he was on holiday.
John Zogby, who does opinion surveys for Reuters, believes polling has become an essential tool of a modern democracy.
"Leaders need to know where public opinion is and where it could be as a result of their actions. Good polling connects politicians to voters and voters to each other," Zogby said.
But Samuel Popkin, who was a member of Clinton's polling team during the first two years of his presidency, said people were sick and tired of polls.

"It's clearly the case that people are going crazy with polls. The sheer number is unbelievable. Newspapers feed their legitimacy by doing too much polling and pollsters themselves start to believe they wield all the power," said Popkin, now a political science professor with the University of California, San Diego.

On the other hand, politicians can get into deep trouble by not polling. Popkin said that the White House did not ask the right questions about Clinton's health care reform plan in 1993 and 1994. The plan crashed to defeat.

Even when the right questions are asked, polls can be deceiving for politicians. Republican House Speaker Newt Gingrich used polls to help determine which items should be included in his Contract with America legislative programme.
The result was a list of initiatives -- balancing the budget, providing a family tax cut, cutting government programmes -- which were popular individually but proved politically deadly when combined.
Said Bruce Blakeman, who conducts polls for Republican candidates: "Politicians on both sides of the aisle are extremely poll-driven, which does not lend itself to strong leadership."
Even Morris concedes the danger. At one point, he recounts a White House strategy meeting at which then chief of staff Leon Panetta resisted some of his proposals.
"Leon muttered that it was a good thing (Abraham) Lincoln didn't have to conduct the Civil War by polls," Morris writes.
